doc.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

title: Bunk Johnson at the Stuyvesant Casino and George Lewis
summary: He saw Bunk Johnson's opening night, got to know George Lewis, and assesses the band's playing and Lewis's later meeting.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: You were in one of them?

You could see me with my first wife, we were still going together. She’s sitting on my knee and we’re smiling listening to Bunk Johnson. It’s a marvelous thing. So I liked it, and I got to know George Lewis rather well. And he hated Bunk Johnson and the whole band hated Bunk. It was like — and George Lewis was such a gentle, sweet guy. But I remember we were in a men’s room once and Bunk’s name came up and he just — Bunk Johnson — you wouldn’t believe that George could get that nasty with those kind of words. I mean that’s how much he disliked Bunk.
Well they were probably thrown together with him because he had so much hype going on, rediscovered, you know, working in the fields, and they got new teeth and all.

Well Bunk was a marvelous musician. Bunk used to call that whole band, Jim Robinson and George Lewis and [Lawrence] Marrero and what’s the name of the piano player, [Alton] Pernell, his wartime emergency band. Because Bunk was a great trumpet player. And I listened to that band critically, I loved the whole sound. But after a while I realized that, Jim Robinson especially, would play through changes, you know [scats] chord changes. Swinging, nice tone and everything and exciting, but he wasn’t making the changes. And George Lewis played out of tune. I loved him, he has a wonderful nice approach, but he wasn’t in the league with an Omer Simeon or Johnny Dodds or Bechet. Same idea but you know. So I got to know that band and I liked him. As a matter of fact in later years when I first went to New Orleans with Louis Armstrong I got a word from Allan Jaffe, the guy that ran Preservation Hall, that, “George wants to see you.” And George, when I first met him in New York he was a mild guy, I think he was afraid to

talk to white people. It was, you know, he came from such a different milieu, you know. I mean it was bad days down there you know. And George once says, isn’t that nice, I’m touched, you know. And so we meet him in the Quarter somewhere and we’re going to go to a funeral. There’s George in a nice suit, Panama hat and a cigarette holder with a cigarette in it. This down home guy, right?
Right and now he’s in his own element.

And we embraced and he’s smiling, you know, it was the whole thing. He said I never thought I’d meet with Louis, and I forget what he said but it was sort of like he was taken with that you know. “Oh I have faith in you all the time.” And years later when I was with Louis Armstrong and we were in San Francisco, we played a thing there, what’s that San Francisco festival, I can’t think. Sacramento.
